chunks: From him, from Sa'd ibn Isma'il, from his father Isma'il ibn Isa, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the skins of cattle; if a man buys them in one of the markets of al-Jabal, should he ask about their slaughter if the seller is a Muslim who is not well-versed? He said: 'You must ask about it if you see polytheists selling it, and if you see them praying in it, then do not ask about it.'

key_terms.يُصَلُّونَ فِيهِ: Praying in it (referring to the skins)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on buying animal skins from Muslim sellers who are not well-versed in religious rites?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Hassan (AS) clarifies the practical application of *istishab* (presumption of continuity) regarding animal skins (*julud*) in market transactions. He instructs that if the seller is a Muslim, one must verify the slaughter (*dhikr*) unless they are known to be polytheists or are observed praying in the skins, in which case the presumption of impurity or non-compliance allows for a relaxed inquiry. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic principle of relying on observable signs of religious identity to determine the ritual status of goods without requiring exhaustive verification in every transaction.
